1: The Anarchist Cookbook. If you had a book like a rebellious teenager's diary crossed with a recipe collection for chaos, then that would be The Anarchist Cookbook. It's a legendary and controversial guidebook that teaches you how to stir up trouble in a kitchen called society. William Powell, the author, blended Han Solo's rebellious nature with Gordon Ramsay's kitchen prowess. Instead of whipping up cupcakes, this book gives you recipes on how to make explosive devices, offering step-by-step guides on making bombs, weapons, and other naughty contraptions. It's like that over-enthusiastic science teacher who accidentally burns down the lab during a fun experiment. Powell wrote this during the troublesome 1970s, which was a time when more people were thinking about rebellion and revolutions as a result of the Cold War. The problem with the anarchist cookbook is that it's not just a theoretical text for rebellious teenagers, it has real-world implications, having been linked to various acts of violence and mischief. As such, authorities weren't thrilled about this guide to chaos and other dangerous things. While critics see it as a danger to society, defenders see it as a misunderstood champion of free expression. But you can't call it a literary masterpiece when you see your kid turning a pipe into a bazooka. The Satanic Verses If you see this book in an everything-must-go backyard sale and buy it, thinking it would help you summon the devil for some infernal deal, you'll be disappointed. It's not a guide for calling up demons, but it's just as controversial within religious circles. The Satanic Versus starts with two dudes surviving an airplane explosion and suddenly start sprouting wings and experiencing hallucinations. They became fantasy creatures, with one turning into an angel, while the other one a devil, as if they were transported into a fantasy RPG game. Gibril, the angel character, relived the life of the Prophet Muhammad, and this is where the controversy starts. The book's reimagining of the Prophet shows how Satan sprinkled a few verses in the Quran here and there, basically turning some of the parts of Islam's holiest book into the work of the devil. It was seen as blasphemous because it fictionalized Muhammad and introduced new controversial interpretations of Islamic history, turning it into the Voldemort of books. You can't even say its name without raising eyebrows. Because of the controversy surrounding it, libraries have hidden it away as if it were a map that leads to a hidden treasure. In 1989, Ayatollah Khomeini of Iran dropped a fatwa, an official Islam ruling, but essentially a death warrant, making the author of this book an outlaw, sending him into hiding from assassins. But it wasn't only because the content was problematic. The ripple effect was the scary part because it sparked protests, debates, and violent reactions from the Islamic community. Religious leaders thought that he was mocking their sacred figures. Imagine someone at your house party throwing around your grandma's ashes. That's how these religious leaders felt about the satanic verses. Despite its controversy, the book is still widely talked about in non-religious circles, proving that you can still be the life of the party, even if you're a party pooper. 120 Days of Sodom 120 Days of Sodom by Marquis de Sade is so scandalous that it makes Fifty Shades of Grey look like a Disney bedtime story. The book isn't just at the top of the list of R-rated stuff, but it's off the charts, somewhere close to XXX in terms of its obscenity. The book tells the story of a group of rich guys holed up in a castle, not for a polite tea party, but to indulge in every depraved fantasy known to humanity, rounding up nine boys and girls and subjecting them to 120 days of unspeakable acts. You're looking at things so obscene that even Johnny Sins wouldn't dare to read this book. Marquis de Sade, the author, didn't hold back Every horrible sexual act from sadism to masochism were served in this book like a buffet of taboos with a side of outrage You can think of it as a circus where morality takes a step back and goes on vacation to give way to insanity, which became the new normal in this story. The book crossed the line and pole vaulted over it, becoming a forbidden novel that could give a nun a heart attack and send her straight to the emergency room. Lady Chatterley's Lover It's the early 1900s in Old England, and every woman is buttoned up from her ankles to her neck. Seeing a bit of skin is the equivalent of seeing a Playboy magazine back then, but here comes D.H. Lawrence with Lady Chatterley's Lover. This forbidden book comes with its fair share of steamy storylines with a dash of immorality. The story follows Lady Chatterley, stuck in a marriage that would make watching paint dry sound very exciting, because she's married to a paralyzed man unable to satisfy her womanly needs and desires. This lady isn't the type to sit around and knit all day. She craves adventure, passion, and a lot of that good old physical attention. But with her husband unable to do anything, she dives headfirst into an affair with the gamekeeper, Melors. Now this guy is your rugged fellow who tends to the woods and looks like he's on the front cover of a men's health magazine. Nothing says frailties of a woman better than a dude with rock-hard abs. But while you'd think that this steamy love affair in the woods upset people about this book, you're only looking at half of this story. Lawrence wrote the book to poke fun at England's rigid class structure and societal norms at a time when there were hardly any differences between a high-class English woman and a nun. It insulted the foundations of England's high society, openly talking about sex and scandalous relationships while showing the differences between people from different classes. The 48 Laws of Power When you combine books written by your manipulative ex and a master of social strategy, you get The 48 Laws of Power by Robert Greene, which may look like a self-help book for climbing the corporate ladder of success, but is dark enough that it's been banned in a lot of different prison systems worldwide. The scoop is that the book introduces different ways for you to use strategies and tactics for success. But these tips aren't your simple wake up early, go to the gym, journal your goals advice you get from the usual TED Talks. Instead, they tell you how to manipulate people, places, and situations to get what you want. For example, one of the laws tells you to conceal your intentions. That's the perfect guide for being the sneakiest person at work. Another law tells you to let someone else do the work for you. It basically tells you to manipulate someone to make life easier. These tactics work wonders in a ruthless game of corporate thrones, where you kill or get killed in the corporate ladder system. But in regular life, it's like you're bringing a bazooka to a snowball fight because it's ultimately overkill for you to be manipulating people in regular day-to-day interactions. Schools and prisons have banned the 48 laws of power out of fear of turning the lunchroom into a scene from Game of Thrones. Minus the backstabbing and the dragons, prisons already have a lot of problems to deal with. From drug lords to murderers, the last thing they need is to turn their inmates into masters of manipulative strategies. Lolita by Vladimir Novikov. Vladimir Novikov is that one friend who can't keep his fantasies to himself, often telling you about the wet dreams he had last night and how he's dying to experience some sick pleasures. Naturally, you'd want to keep your ears covered the entire time, but he tells such a good story that you can't help but listen to him. That's what you get from Novikov's book Lolita. The book drops readers into the mind of a character named Humbert Humber, a seriously twisted guy obsessed with a 12-year-old girl named Dolores Hayes, aka Lolita It like watching a train wreck in slow motion because you know that Humbert moral compass is bound to crash and burn Imagine telling your family that you reading a book about a guy who sees a child as a seductive nymph he can resist It may be a literary masterpiece in terms of its writing and narrative but you can't accept the twisted ideas surrounding a story about a grown man in love with a girl barely in her teens. But Nabokov's writing isn't just awkwardly flirting with pedophilia, it's also about how he is like a tragic clown who keeps tripping over his own bad decisions, and you find yourself oddly rooting for this bumbling mess. Throughout that time, you get a sneak preview into the darkest corners of his mind as he's trying to justify his obsession. The writer's genius lies in how he makes you squirm with discomfort while you marvel at his literary gifts. It makes you admire something you shouldn't be admiring, and that can be dangerous to a society that wants its kids to be kids instead of sex symbols. It's like you're introducing porn to a monk, potentially affecting his moral compass forever. Brave New World Let's say you live in a world where everyone is happy, a little too happy. That's what you get in a book where everyone is forced to stay in line with little to no hope of getting out of that bubble. Aldous Huxley's book Brave New World describes a society where people in this new world were forced to get hooked on a literal happy pill called Soma, which made them happy, suppressing deep emotions. It's also a world where society has an entire assembly line churning babies out like designer shoes. You get assigned to a cast, like it's a Hogwarts sorting hat ceremony. The government even controls your love life. It's like they control your Tinder account, swiping left until they see a person who would match you, forcing you to marry them. Put yourself in a world where society runs on consumerism, instant gratification, and tech control. Sound familiar? It's like our lives, but with extra drama. We've got smartphones and social media keeping us perpetually distracted, just like the novel's characters. Algorithms tell us what to think and feel, kind of like the government's puppet show in the book. It's like living in a dystopian sitcom where the punchline is our own life. Governments worldwide looked at this book and said, hmm, this Huxley guy might be onto something. Let's not give anyone any ideas. It's like they're worried we might trade freedom for the convenience that people get in Brave New World. Naturally, it found its place in the forbidden library of taboo books. But from how things are going, Brave New World seems more of a cautionary tale that's already predicted the future for us. Who knows what Elon's Neuralink will do to our brains one day? Animal Farm George Orwell's Animal Farm puts you in an old McDonald had a farm nursery rhyme that gets darker. The animals on this farm had enough of humans bossing them around, eventually kicking them out, and started running things themselves. No humans, no problems, right? That sounds like a great place for Porky and his pals to live in, but Orwell's book swiped at society through his fluffy tale of barnyard politics. The story revolves around how the pigs at the farm eventually took power, becoming the new head hogs. So from telling the chickens and everyone else that all animals are equal, these oinkers thought that they were better than everyone else, taking the place of the humans as the new oppressors. They turned the farm into a pig pen of oppression and inequality. In other words, Orwell was telling a story about how revolutions that try to give power back to the people will only lead to new dictators rising. The book is a satire that pokes fun at power-hungry leaders who promise equality but decide that they deserve more than everyone else. Governments who saw what Orwell was trying to do felt that Animal Farm was not just airing their dirty laundry but also throwing it out for everyone, Fearing it might inspire people to start looking at their leaders as less noble steeds and more like pigs. If you think that you have barnyard animals or pets seemingly plotting your downfall you might want to share your thoughts with us by joining our Discord The Grapes of Wrath You think a book about grapes is as wholesome as biting into a batch of sweet fruit However The Grapes of Wrath by John Steinbeck makes you think that you're eating sour grapes that could turn your face upside down instantly. First, the book gives the Jode family's woes the spotlight in the most unflattering way possible. Set during the Great Depression, it's like Steinbeck decided to cast farmers as the villains of the agricultural world, complete with sinister mustaches and brooding glares. Instead of being your friendly neighborhood food producers, he turned them from farm heroes into sourpusses, making it seem like they harvested frowns instead of potatoes. The language and themes in the book were also as juicy as overripe grapes. There were plenty of scenes of violence, harsh realities, and profanity that were too sensitive for the mind of the regular 1940s American. Conservative readers would have wanted to go to church to confess that they read The Grapes of Wrath. As such, authorities feared that the book might corrupt the minds of the innocent and the youth, turning their brains into a chaotic fruit salad of rebellious thoughts. Then there was the belief that the book seemed un-American. It criticized capitalism, looking like it was a bit too red for comfort during a time when Americans feared the spread of communism. Slaughterhouse-Five The first thing you'd usually hear from people who've heard about Kurt Vonnegut's Slaughterhouse Five is that it's that book about time traveling and aliens. But there's a deeper reason why this novel found itself in the dimension of banned books. It's basically about a soldier who got so lost in time that he traveled from one era to another, playing hopscotch through history, but with explosions. At one point, he's a POW in Dresden, Germany during its infamous bombing, and the book paints it under the worst lighting possible. Written during the Cold War when the government tried to convince everyone that fighting communists was as American as apple pie, this book was like the literary equivalent of someone wearing a make love not war t-shirt to a military parade. The feds probably thought it was a sneaky hippie manifesto, secretly encouraging people to swap their rifles for daisies. Some readers found the book unbearable because Vonnegut boldly mixed existential dread with dark humor. People were not ready for that brand of comedy, especially when things became a bit too real for readers. So the book's banishment is mostly due to its audacious blend of satire, science fiction, and uncomfortable truths. In the grand theater of literature, it's the play that makes people question what they saw and rethink their beliefs. And during the 70s, it just wasn't what the government wanted people to feel. Invisible Man Written by Ralph Ellison during the 1950s, the book was so loud that it was like bringing a karaoke machine to a mime party. It loved diving deep into racial identity and societal invisibility while airing dirty secrets and subjects that were once considered taboo. The book's exploration of race and identity stirred the pot during an era when black people were still second-class citizens. No one wanted to read a book with a surprise lecture about politics if they expected a party, and that was what Invisible Man was all about. It's like you realized your favorite TV show is actually a documentary on a boring topic, like industrial waste. Then there's the language and themes that were a bit too much for the 1950s mind. The book tackles violence, exploitation, and discrimination, which used to be as awkward as talking about your non-existent girlfriend in the middle of a family dinner. It was a little too raw and honest, making everyone question everything they knew about society. The vulgar nature of the novel forced schools to expel it from their library quickly, turning Invisible Man into an invisible book.

1: Monarchy A monarchy is a type of government ruled by a monarch, which is often a king or a queen. The monarch's role is passed down through the same family, from generation to generation, often going to the oldest child. Major countries operating under a monarchy include the United Kingdom, Japan, Spain, Sweden, and Saudi Arabia. There are multiple forms of monarchies, for example, symbolic monarchy, where the monarch has no political or economic power like the United Kingdom. Instead, the country is run by a parliamentary government led by a prime minister. On the other hand, an absolute monarchy is where the king or queen has the power to make all the important decisions in a country. The disadvantage of a monarchy is that it can lead to unsuitable leaders who came to power because they were the heirs. This often leads to a lack of democratic governance and the potential for abuse of power. Socialism Socialism is a form of government wherein the workers or laborers are allowed to own property, but the distribution of goods and services is controlled by a central government. The government's goal is to distribute all of the goods and services equally to ensure everyone in the country has the same opportunities as everyone else. Some of the more common examples of socialist states are the People's Republic of China and the Republic of Cuba. While most socialist states call themselves republics, they usually follow the fundamentals of socialism, where labor and property are equitably distributed and there are no social classes or hierarchies. The reason why socialism is not as popular as some forms of government is the lack of incentives. If someone gets the same resources as someone who didn't work as hard, there's no point in working harder. This can potentially lead to the nation's failure, especially if no one is willing to work hard to get better incentives. Democracy A democracy is when a country believes that the citizens are the supreme rulers of the nation. Democracy is as old as human civilization itself, but first appeared in the ancient political and philosophical teachings of the people of Athens. In a democracy, the people are the ones who determine the leaders and the laws of the land through a majority vote. It also provides an environment wherein fundamental human rights are respected, and the people are allowed to exercise their free will. Some of the most democratic countries in the world include Norway, Sweden, and New Zealand. However, the problem in a democratic country is that it can be too unstable due to constant leadership changes. Autocracy An autocracy is when only one person or ruling party holds supreme power over an entire nation. Every decision that the autocratic ruler makes cannot be limited by external factors. These decisions are absolute and should be followed by the country. The autocrat also has total control over what the people can do when it comes to their civil liberties. In an autocracy, the people have no say in the nation's affairs, contrasting it to democracy. Autocracies have existed since ancient times usually in absolute monarchies where the king word is the law The Soviet Union once ruled by Joseph Stalin is one of the more recent examples of an autocracy. The biggest disadvantage of an autocracy is the potential abuse of power by the autocrat, who may become a dictator. Federal Federal governments formally divide the sovereign power between a central government and the regions that form part of the country. The central government is still the leader of the whole nation but allows the different regions or states to have control over their internal affairs. These states can have their leaders and laws but are not independent nations. The reason why federalism wants to decentralize some of the functions of the government is to promote efficiency. This is usually the case for bigger countries because it's easier for smaller territories to govern themselves than allowing a central government to govern an entire nation. It's similar to how the head coach of a sports team needs to delegate roles to his assistant coaches. The assistant coaches have a sense of independence in their roles, but they are still under the overall leadership of the head coach. The most common example of a federal government is the United States of America, which is under the leadership of a president but has different state senators that manage their territories and constituents. One of the biggest drawbacks of a federal form of government is the possible economic inequality between different regions, because some territories have better access to certain resources that other territories can't have access to. Oligarchy. Oligarchy, which can be translated to rule of the few, is a form of government wherein only a few oligarchs have power over the entire nation. These oligarchs come from different groups or families that usually rise to power through financial or military means. The country's political, social, and economic affairs are settled through the decisions made by the oligarchs. Oligarchies, unlike monarchies, don't formally pass their leadership roles to the next generation, but can still stay in power for multiple generations as long as they maintain their financial or military status within the nation. The USA is formally a federal government, but is often seen as an oligarchy by most people because of the influence that large corporations have on the decisions of politicians. Modern-day oligarchies often arise when large firms and businesses become too financially powerful. The worst part about oligarchies is the potential economic and social inequalities between different classes. Only the rich and powerful benefit from decisions made by their fellow oligarchs. Republic The concept of the republic results from the ancient Greek philosopher Plato's teachings and has become the foundation of many modern forms of government. In a republic, the people have the right to the affairs of the country because it is believed that the state belongs to the people and everyone in the state has an equal opportunity to take part in the country's decisions. It is only through the will of the people that the leaders of a country are elected into office. The leaders of a republic are representatives of the people and should be making decisions that favor everyone in the state There are notable differences between a republic and a democracy In a republic the people own the state On the other hand, in a pure democracy, the people don't own the state but are the sovereign leaders of the nation. A country can be both a republic and a democracy simultaneously. For example, the Philippines is both a republic and a democracy, but not all countries are republics and democracies at the same time. Canada is a democracy but is constitutionally a monarchy. Republics also have their drawbacks because not all nations are culturally and socially suited for a republic form of government, especially if corruption and abuses are common among the leaders. Communist A communist government believes in the concept of a classless society and aims to achieve it through the state's absolute control over the country's resources. The ruling party, often led by an authoritarian figure, controls all of the social, political, and economic decision-making in a communist nation. Communist countries believe in Karl Marx's teachings that a capitalist form of government would eventually destroy itself. As a result, the goal of communism is to achieve a classless society through the elimination of private ownership of property so that all goods and services within the state are equally shared by the people. There are currently five countries that practice communism in today's modern world, namely China, Cuba, Laos, North Korea, and Vietnam. One of the reasons why communism often fails is that it is prone to abuses and the restriction of human rights. Anarchism Anarchies are often called non-governance because the key aspect of this form of government is the absence of a central government. The goal of an anarchist system is to not only decentralize the power of the government, but to eliminate the government itself, to allow the people to self-govern. The popular belief is that an anarchist government tends to be chaotic. But that's not the case, because one of the most important goals of anarchism is to allow people to volunteer willingly and freely to help one another for the improvement of the community. It is different from socialism or communism because there is no equitable distribution of labor and resources, but there exists an equitable right to self-governance. In most cases, anarchies rise from destroying a previous government just before establishing a new form of government. There is no true anarchist government today, but Somalia was in anarchy before 2006 when it had no national government. The problem with anarchism is that it can lead to chaos when everyone is only looking after their self-interests instead of helping one another. Presidential In a presidential form of government, there is a separation between the different branches of the government, allowing the executive branch to have separate roles from the legislature. The president is the head of the executive branch and is tasked with the execution of the laws. Meanwhile the legislature is the branch that responsible for the enactment of the laws Presidential governments can arise from republics and democracies Most democratic republics have a presidential form of government Some of the best examples of presidential governments are South Korea, the Philippines, Nigeria, and Indonesia. A presidential form of government's major downside is that too much executive power in one person can lead to abuse of power. Parliamentary In a parliamentary system of government, the party with the greatest representation in the legislature is nominated to the executive branch. The party's leader becomes the prime minister or the chancellor who appoints members of the party to the cabinet to have their tasks as members of the executive branch. However, the ruling party does not hold absolute executive powers because the opposing party must challenge the ruling party regularly. The prime minister can also be removed from power at the will of the legislature or the ruling party through a vote of no confidence if the prime minister fails to uphold their duties. Parliamentary systems can also exist alongside different forms of government, such as a monarchy. Japan is a constitutional monarchy with a royal family acting as symbolic leaders, but has a parliamentary government led by a prime minister. The problem with a parliamentary form of government is that it fails to provide a stable government because the opposing party will always try to challenge the ruling party, leading to never-ending conflicts. Constitutional A constitutional form of government is when a constitution acts as the foundation of the country's laws and systems. It is the constitution that defines the limits and functions of a government. In most cases, the constitution is enacted to extend the people's will. Constitutional governments come in many forms. For example, the United Kingdom is a constitutional monarchy that defines the limits of the monarch's powers. The United States is also a constitutional government but is a presidential form of constitutional democracy. However, the major weakness of a constitutional form of government is that every system or law in place has to be consistent with the constitution. The constitution has to be amended if vital laws need to be passed but are inconsistent with the constitution. Totalitarian The term totalitarian was originally coined by Benito Mussolini, who led the fascist state of Italy during his reign from the 1920s to the 1940s. A totalitarian system of government is when the government seeks to control everything within the country. This does not only include the political and economic matters of the country, but also the beliefs and values of the citizens. Theoretically, the freedom of the citizens in a totalitarian regime is suppressed. Totalitarian government abides by the belief that everything within the state should fall under the control of the state and that no one in the state should ever go against the state. One of the best examples of a totalitarian regime in modern times is North Korea, which follows a totalitarian republic ruled by the Kim family for three generations already. Like socialist, autocratic, and communist governments, a totalitarian regime is prone to human rights suppression and abuses. Thank you.
